crime.value: Murder disguised as a hunting accident: Cozenka shoots her husband at night claiming she mistook him for the escaped 'vicious' leopard Demon. Central question: was the cat actually dangerous, i.e. was the shooting truly a mistake?
crime.quote: "Cozenka shot Ken. She thought he was Demon. She thought he had green eyes."

victim.value: Ken Bender, clumsy, boring Texas oil millionaire who married Cozenka; killable because his vast fortune passed to a wife who loved another man and only wanted his money
victim.quote: "He was rich as Croesus... you were quite willing to take everything he had except the one thing he wanted you most to accept. Himself."

closed_world.value: Bender's isolated twenty-room lodge and private African animal preserve, twenty miles from a whistle stop in the remote Southwest, with only the three principals, the narrator and a small staff present
closed_world.quote: "picked up at a lonely whistle stop and driven twenty miles to Ken Bender's place"

culprit_and_motive.value: Cozenka fired the shot with Peter Wyndham as co-conspirator (he secretly tamed Demon, then shot the cat to destroy the evidence); motive was Bender's money and her love for Wyndham
culprit_and_motive.quote: "Your darling said you two were planning to kill him."

resolution.value: Only partial: Payne reasons that the missing footage of Demon must exist, finds a hidden 16mm reel showing the leopard tamed and purring; the inquest jury calls for further investigation, but the grand jury refuses to indict. Both culprits die within six months (buffalo, car crash) — order restored by chance, not justice
resolution.quote: "The grand jury, upon advice of the County Attorney, refused to indict."

investigator.value: Marty Payne, a magazine writer and houseguest — an outsider witness who becomes amateur accuser; official counterpart Sheriff Henderson and coroner Doctor Wendell
investigator.quote: "I was even witness to the tragedy in a professional capacity."

suspect_architecture.value: Small closed cast of three principals plus narrator: Cozenka (Eurasian wife, motive: inherited millions and freedom from a bore she never loved, opportunity: fired the shot), Peter Wyndham (her lover/white hunter, motive: her money, opportunity: staged the 'vicious' cat and shot Demon to destroy evidence), Ken Bender (the wealthy husband, victim), and Marty Payne (journalist-witness). Guilt is joint; no genuine alternative suspect exists — the 'suspect' offered to the world is the leopard itself.
suspect_architecture.quote: "Your darling said you two were planning to kill him."

red_herring.value: The black leopard Demon, deliberately presented as savage and treacherous so the shooting would read as a hunting accident; reinforced by Wyndham's staged warning at the cage and by shooting the cat afterward to remove the only living disproof.
red_herring.quote: "those cats are the soul of treachery—that one in particular. A little closer and you could have lost an arm."

clue_fairness.value: Fair-play: the reader sees every clue as Payne does — the couple standing 'very close,' Wyndham's over-emphatic warning, Bender's confided fear, and above all the leopard's tame visit to the den before the shot; the hidden taming film is deduced from the reader-visible absence of Demon from the Africa footage.
clue_fairness.quote: "it seemed strange to me that the leopard did not appear anywhere in the hour-long film covering her last trip to Africa"

social_world.value: Texas oil money and celebrity glamour: an ungainly self-made millionaire buys an African replica preserve for his exotic wife, who keeps a hired 'guide and companion' on the payroll; local law and grand jury defer to wealth, beauty and the battery of defense attorneys money can buy, while the outsider writer has no standing.
social_world.quote: "the merging of oriental loveliness with Texas oil millions"

alibi.value: No conventional alibi; instead a shared cover story — 'we were hunting separately, I mistook him for the leopard's green eyes' — an accident claim rather than a whereabouts denial, corroborated by Wyndham's account of tracking and killing the cat.
alibi.quote: "We were hunting separately. I was not using my light—watching for the glow of Demon's eyes."

reveal_mechanic.value: Physical demonstration at the coroner's inquest: the concealed sixteen-millimeter reel of Demon's taming, screened with sound track showing Cozenka frolicking with the gentle cat and the animal purring — proving the beast was tame and the 'accident' impossible.
reveal_mechanic.quote: "I think you will agree, Sheriff, that the cat is purring, not snarling."

media_and_audience.value: The crime unfolds inside a manufactured press romance — Cozenka and Bender are national magazine property, and public sympathy for the glamorous widow neutralizes the accusation; the sheriff distrusts Payne precisely as a story-hungry 'newshawk,' and the jury pool would never convict her.
media_and_audience.quote: "Would you care to go before a jury made up principally of men and try to get Cozenka Bender convicted"

investigator_wound.value: Payne is a journalist who profits from other people's sensations; the case exploits his guilt at having passively watched, dismissed Bender's plea for help, and possibly courted the story — plus his own susceptibility to Cozenka's beauty and his fear for his career.
investigator_wound.quote: "perhaps I was subconsciously conditioned to stand back and let it all happen."

victims_enemies.value: Ken Bender is undone by the two people closest to him: his wife Cozenka, who took his oil millions but found him a 'crashing bore' and loved his guide instead, and Peter Wyndham, the handsome 'white hunter' whom Bender complaisantly accepted as his wife's constant companion. The grievance is not hatred but suffocated contempt — he loved her hopelessly, and she resented owing everything to a clumsy, childlike man.
victims_enemies.quote: “But all his love and money couldn’t change the fact that he was a crashing bore—a big, clumsy, childlike man”

suspect_wounds.value: Cozenka's vulnerability is her genuine affection for the leopard Demon — the one sincere feeling in her performance — which forced her to hide the film of the tame cat rather than destroy it, and to protest its screening in a way that betrayed her. Wyndham's is his cultivated self-control: his over-eager warning about the cat's 'treachery' and his desperate haste to shoot Demon read as guilt. Marty Payne himself is wounded by his trade — a magazine writer sensation-hunting, which the sheriff uses to discount him.
suspect_wounds.quote: “That film is most personal. I beg you not to run it off. You have no right to shame me!”

unreliable_frame.value: Marty Payne narrates, and opens by admitting he may have subconsciously let the tragedy happen for the sake of a story; he closes conceding he might have been wrong from the beginning. Cozenka and Wyndham give a coordinated false account of the shooting; Cozenka's grief is explicitly judged by Payne as acting.
unreliable_frame.quote: “So perhaps I was subconsciously conditioned to stand back and let it all happen. I hope not, but I can’t be sure.”

setting_as_constraint.value: Bender's isolated Texas ranch, twenty miles from a whistle stop, remade into a private African replica stocked with dangerous game. The remoteness means no independent witnesses, the nearest law is a half-hour away in Kenton, and the presence of a 'savage' black leopard supplies a ready-made explanation for a night shooting during a hunt with lights off.
setting_as_constraint.quote: “driven twenty miles to Ken Bender’s place” ... “The County Sheriff. He comes from Kenton—a small village. A half hour’s drive.”

evidence_type.value: Documentary/film evidence: a reel of sixteen-millimeter film with sound track, found in Cozenka's closet, showing Wyndham taming Demon and Cozenka playing with the gentle, purring cat — deduced from the suspicious absence of the leopard from her hour-long Africa footage. Supported only by Payne's testimonial account of the tame cat visiting him.
evidence_type.quote: “took from my pocket the reel of sixteen-millimeter film I’d found on a shelf in one of Cozenka’s closets”

false_suspect.value: Demon, the black leopard — deliberately framed by the culprits as a treacherous killer whose supposed green-eyed charge explains the 'accidental' shot; Wyndham then kills it to destroy the only witness to its tameness.
false_suspect.quote: “those cats are the soul of treachery—that one in particular. A little closer and you could have lost an arm.”

technical_detail.value: Big-cat handling: a jungle cat can in fact be tamed, and Wyndham had secretly done so in Africa, filming the process. The murder method depends on the public belief that leopards are irredeemably vicious — the cat's reputation makes a night 'hunt' with lights off plausible and the mis-aimed shot excusable. Exposure comes from the same knowledge: the cat that visited Payne behaved like a kitten, and the soundtrack records purring, not snarling.
technical_detail.quote: “I think you will agree, Sheriff, that the cat is purring, not snarling.”

moral_ambiguity.value: Cozenka is not a simple monster: she genuinely loved the leopard and mourned sacrificing it, and she loved Wyndham as hopelessly as Bender loved her — trapped in the same unreciprocated devotion she inflicted. Payne, meanwhile, admits he would not want to 'pull the switch' on either of them on the evidence he had, and the sheriff's refusal to prosecute is presented as sound legal logic rather than corruption.
moral_ambiguity.quote: “I think she truly loved Wyndham; ironically, in the same hopeless way Bender had loved her.”
